title: No fast, no Ramadan: the One served
hookLine: Guru Arjan sings that he keeps no fast of one faith or the other but serves the One alone (Bhairao M5, ang 1136)
carry: one master, called gosain and allah

cards: A street in Lahore or Amritsar in Guru Arjan's day. One neighbor is keeping a Hindu fast. Another is keeping the fast of Ramadan.

Both are serious, both devout, and both might well ask the Guru's Sikhs: so which do you keep? In Raga Bhairao, on Ang eleven hundred thirty-six, Guru Arjan answers. He doesn't mock either fast, and he doesn't pick one.
He names, instead, whom he serves.

teach.b: On day six, the question was whether Sikhs are Hindu or Muslim; here a Guru answers in a hymn. Its opening, paraphrased: I keep no fast, nor the month of Ramadan; I serve the One who protects me in the end.
And then: the one Master, Gosain and Allah, is mine. Gosain is a name for God from Hindu speech; Allah is the name in Muslim speech. The Guru uses both, for one Lord.
The hymn goes on to say he doesn't go on pilgrimage to Mecca or worship at Hindu holy places, and later, paraphrased: I am neither Hindu nor Muslim; my body and breath belong to Allah and Ram.
It's easy to hear this as a rejection.
Read in its setting, it's a statement of where the Guru stands: not against his neighbors, not ranking their devotion, but naming a path given wholly to the One, whatever name the One is called by.
Sevi, I serve, is the working word. Service, seva, runs through the Gurus' teaching, and the hymn makes the One the only master of that service.
This week has followed one thread in different clothes: the Gatha, the Funhe, the Chaubole, the Mundavani's plate, the Lord standing up to finish the work, a will received as sweet.
And now, the One served by all of it. Different forms, one direction.

how: This hymn of Guru Arjan in Raga Bhairao is often quoted when Sikhs explain their path as distinct and devoted to the One; in the gurdwara it is sung in kirtan and explained in katha.

o: giving your service wholly to God, by whatever name
keeping both the Hindu and Muslim fasts each year
obeying one human ruler above every other law

games.q: inside the hymn: tap the pairs.
p: a name for God from Hindu speech

s: the hymn mocks the fasts of Guru Arjan's neighbors
it doesn't rank or mock; it names whom the Guru serves: the One who protects in the end.
the hymn uses both Hindu and Muslim names for one Lord
Gosain and Allah, it says, are one Master, and body and breath belong to Allah and Ram.

games.q: two devout neighbors keep two different fasts, and someone asks Guru Arjan which one he keeps. what does the hymn say?
o: he keeps the fast of Ramadan.
neither; he serves the One who protects in the end.
games.why: he picks neither and mocks neither: he names a path given wholly to the One, called by both Hindu and Muslim names.

practice: Bring to mind whoever or whatever your life is most given to: for some it's God, for some a child, a parent, a calling.
Hold that one in your attention and let a small service you could offer come to you, a chore, a call, a quiet act of care, without chasing it. If you pray, rest in Waheguru on each out-breath.

wordCard.voice: Serving the One. Guru Arjan's hymn in Raga Bhairao: no fast of one faith or the other; I serve the One who protects me in the end. Today's word.

orig.note: Him I serve: Guru Arjan's answer in Raga Bhairao, Ang 1136.

carryVoice: Your line: one Master, called Gosain and Allah. That closes a week of Guru Arjan's shorter forms and his seal. Rest well.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Bhairao Mahala 5, Ang 1136 (varat na rahau na mah ramadana; tis sevi jo rakhai nidana; na ham Hindu na Musalman)
